title: Titus Andronicus
description: Shakespeare's first tragedy, written in collaboration with George Peele: the Roman general Titus returns from the Goths with the captive queen Tamora, whose revenge — the rape and mutilation of Titus's daughter Lavinia, the deaths of his sons — drives the play to its banquet of horrors, where Titus serves Tamora her own sons baked in a pie.
plot_or_argument: Titus sacrifices Tamora's son and refuses the empire; Tamora, empress through Saturninus, avenges herself through her lover Aaron and her sons Chiron and Demetrius; Titus feigns madness, discovers the rapists, and executes his revenge in the cannibal banquet that ends the play.
narrative_structure: A Senecan revenge tragedy of symmetrical atrocity and counter-atrocity, with Aaron the Moor as its gleeful vice-figure.
principal_characters: Titus Andronicus; Tamora; Aaron the Moor; Lavinia; Saturninus; Bassianus; Marcus Andronicus; Lucius; Chiron; Demetrius; young Lucius
meter_and_prosody: Early verse of rhetorical set pieces — Lavinia's mute testimony, Titus's mad wordplay — with Ovid's Metamorphoses as the play's internal book of horrors.
historical_context: Performed from 1594 and printed the same year; its extreme violence answered the vogue for Senecan blood inaugurated by Kyd's Spanish Tragedy.
literary_significance: The most performed of the early tragedies and a laboratory of Shakespeare's tragic art — revenge, madness, and the stage as charnel house.
attribution_notes: George Peele's co-authorship of Act 1 (and possibly other scenes) is now widely accepted on stylistic evidence.
bibliographical_notes: Quarto, 1594; First Folio, 1623. Standard edition: The Oxford Shakespeare: The Complete Works, 2nd edition (2005).

title: Romeo and Juliet
alternative_titles: The Most Excellent and Lamentable Tragedy of Romeo and Juliet
description: Shakespeare's lyric tragedy of young love: the star-crossed children of Verona's feuding houses meet at the Capulet feast, marry in secret, and are destroyed by chance and haste — the deaths of Mercutio and Tybalt, the exile, the sleeping potion, and the double suicide in the tomb that reconciles the houses too late.
plot_or_argument: Romeo and Juliet fall in love across the family feud; Friar Laurence marries them; the street brawl kills Mercutio and Tybalt and exiles Romeo; the Capulets press Paris's suit; Juliet takes the friar's potion; the undelivered letter dooms the lovers; and the play ends with the discovery in the tomb and the prince's judgment on 'a glooming peace'.
narrative_structure: A five-act tragedy of accelerating momentum — comedy in the first two acts, catastrophe in the last — built on the sonnet-form exchanges of the lovers and the antitheses of love and hate.
principal_characters: Romeo; Juliet; Friar Laurence; Mercutio; Tybalt; the Nurse; Benvolio; Lord and Lady Capulet; Lord and Lady Montague; Paris; Prince Escalus
meter_and_prosody: The lovers' first dialogue is a shared sonnet; the play's verse runs from Mercutio's prose fantasia on Queen Mab to Juliet's aubade, with the final couplets of the tomb scene.
historical_context: Written about 1595–96 from Arthur Brooke's poem Romeus and Juliet (1562) via continental novella; printed in quarto in 1597 and in a fuller text in 1599.
literary_significance: The archetype of the love tragedy in world literature — the play that fixed 'star-crossed lovers' in the language and on every subsequent stage and screen.
bibliographical_notes: Quartos 1597, 1599; First Folio, 1623. Standard edition: The Oxford Shakespeare: The Complete Works, 2nd edition (2005).

title: Julius Caesar
description: Shakespeare's Roman tragedy of the republic's death: Brutus, honour's fool, joins the conspiracy against Caesar for Rome's sake; Caesar falls at the Capitol; Antony's funeral oration turns the crowd; and the play moves through the proscriptions and the quarrel of the conspirators to Philippi, where Brutus and Cassius die on their own swords.
plot_or_argument: Cassius seduces Brutus into the conspiracy; Caesar, warned by the soothsayer and Calpurnia's dream, goes to the Senate and is murdered; Antony's 'Friends, Romans, countrymen' speech swings the mob to vengeance; the triumvirate proscribes its enemies; and the battles of Philippi complete the tragedy of Brutus, the noblest Roman of them all.
narrative_structure: A two-part structure of conspiracy and war hinged on the assassination, with the funeral orations as the pivot of the play's rhetoric and the ghost of Caesar as its revenant.
principal_characters: Julius Caesar; Brutus; Cassius; Mark Antony; Portia; Calpurnia; Casca; Octavius Caesar; Cicero; Decius Brutus; the Soothsayer; Cinna the poet
meter_and_prosody: A restrained, 'Roman' verse — no rhyme — with the prose of the plebeians and the two great orations as the peaks of its rhetoric.
historical_context: Written 1599, the year of Essex's fall, from North's Plutarch; its anatomy of mob, coup, and civil war spoke to a court obsessed with succession and rebellion.
literary_significance: The schoolroom tragedy of the English-speaking world — the standard by which political drama, and political oratory, have been measured ever since.
bibliographical_notes: First printed in the First Folio, 1623. Standard edition: The Oxford Shakespeare: The Complete Works, 2nd edition (2005).

title: Hamlet
alternative_titles: The Tragedy of Hamlet, Prince of Denmark
description: Shakespeare's tragedy of revenge and consciousness: the ghost of Hamlet's father charges him to avenge his murder by Claudius, who now wears the crown and the queen; Hamlet's feigned madness, the play-within-the-play ('The Mousetrap'), the deaths of Polonius and Ophelia, and the final duel — poisoned rapier and cup — in which the stage is cleared of the whole royal house.
plot_or_argument: Hamlet tests the ghost's word by staging a murder-play before the king; Claudius's guilt is exposed; Hamlet spares the praying king, kills Polonius, is sent to England with a death warrant he reverses; Ophelia drowns; Laertes returns for revenge; and the poisoned duel at Elsinore kills Gertrude, Laertes, Claudius, and Hamlet himself, with Fortinbras inheriting Denmark.
narrative_structure: A five-act revenge tragedy infinitely deferred and interiorized — soliloquies, plays, and feigned madness displacing action — until the catastrophe of Act 5.
principal_characters: Hamlet; Claudius; Gertrude; the Ghost; Polonius; Ophelia; Laertes; Horatio; Rosencrantz; Guildenstern; Fortinbras; Osric; the First Gravedigger
meter_and_prosody: The widest range in Shakespeare — soliloquy, prose, song, the Player's speech, the graveyard quibbles — with 'To be or not to be' at its centre.
historical_context: Written about 1600–01 in the wake of the lost ur-Hamlet and of the death of Shakespeare's son Hamnet; the three texts (Q1 1603, Q2 1604–05, F 1623) present the classic problem of Shakespearean textual scholarship.
literary_significance: The most famous play ever written — the tragedy of modern consciousness itself, and the summit of the English language's claim on world literature.
attribution_notes: Uncontested; the relationship of the three early texts remains the central problem of its bibliography.
bibliographical_notes: Quarto, 1603 (Q1); Quarto, 1604–05 (Q2); First Folio, 1623. Standard edition: The Oxford Shakespeare: The Complete Works, 2nd edition (2005).

title: Othello
alternative_titles: The Tragedy of Othello, the Moor of Venice
description: Shakespeare's tragedy of jealousy: the Moorish general Othello, married secretly to Desdemona, is undone by his ensign Iago — 'honest Iago' — whose insinuations about Cassio and the handkerchief persuade him of his wife's infidelity, until the murder in the marriage bed and the discovery of Iago's villainy leave Othello to execute judgment on himself.
plot_or_argument: Iago, denied promotion, plots against Othello: he makes Cassio drunk and cashiered, then uses the dropped handkerchief to 'prove' Desdemona's adultery; Othello's jealousy mounts through the eavesdropping scene to the murder of Desdemona; Emilia exposes Iago, who kills her and is taken for torture; Othello, recognizing what he has destroyed, stabs himself on the bed.
narrative_structure: The most tightly constructed of the tragedies — a single plot of insinuation compressed into some thirty-six hours, with Iago's soliloquies as its engine.
principal_characters: Othello; Desdemona; Iago; Emilia; Cassio; Roderigo; Brabantio; Bianca; the Duke of Venice; Lodovico; Montano
meter_and_prosody: Othello's 'Othello music' — the great periodic verse of the senate speech and the farewell to the 'Pride, pomp, and circumstance of glorious war' — against Iago's prose of reduction.
historical_context: Performed at court, 1 November 1604; its sources are Cinthio's novella of the Moor and the Venetian setting of the Cyprus wars; its treatment of race has made it the most urgently debated of the tragedies.
literary_significance: The definitive study of jealousy and of the will to destroy — the most painful, because the most intimate, of the great tragedies.
bibliographical_notes: Quarto, 1622; First Folio, 1623. Standard edition: The Oxford Shakespeare: The Complete Works, 2nd edition (2005).

title: King Lear
description: Shakespeare's tragedy of divided kingdom and broken nature: Lear abdicates, dividing Britain between the daughters who flatter him and disinheriting the one who loves him; cast out by Goneril and Regan, he goes mad on the heath in the storm with his Fool and the disguised Edgar, while the parallel plot of Gloucester and his sons runs to the blinding at Cornwall's hands — and the end brings Cordelia's death and Lear's over her body.
plot_or_argument: Lear's love-test sets the tragedy in motion; Goneril and Regan strip him of his hundred knights; he rages into the storm, meets 'poor Tom' (Edgar), and is saved by Cordelia's French army; Gloucester, betrayed by Edmund and blinded, is led by Edgar to Dover; the battle is lost, Cordelia is hanged, and Lear dies of grief, leaving Edgar and Albany to close the play with its bleakest lines.
narrative_structure: A double plot of Lear and Gloucester mirroring each other, built on the medieval morality pattern inverted — the trial of the daughters, the hovel, the cliff — and ending in the catastrophe that refuses consolation.
principal_characters: King Lear; Goneril; Regan; Cordelia; the Fool; the Earl of Gloucester; Edgar (Poor Tom); Edmund; the Duke of Albany; the Duke of Cornwall; Kent (Caius); Oswald; the King of France
meter_and_prosody: A verse pushed to the edge of its resources — the storm scenes, Lear's curses, Edgar's mad speech, and the spare final lines — with prose for madness and the Fool's riddles.
historical_context: Performed at court, 26 December 1606; the play draws on the old Leir play, Holinshed, and Sidney's Arcadia, and its two early texts (Quarto 1608 and Folio 1623) differ substantially.
literary_significance: By common consent the greatest tragedy in the language — the play that tests the limits of what tragedy can say about nature, justice, and the gods.
attribution_notes: Uncontested; the Quarto/Folio textual divergence is the play's standing editorial problem.
bibliographical_notes: Quarto, 1608; First Folio, 1623. Standard edition: The Oxford Shakespeare: The Complete Works, 2nd edition (2005).

title: Macbeth
description: Shakespeare's shortest tragedy, of ambition and the supernatural: the Scottish general Macbeth, told by the Weird Sisters that he shall be king, murders Duncan in his sleep and enters a reign of blood — Banquo's murder, the apparitions' riddling prophecies, the slaughter of Macduff's family — until Birnam Wood comes to Dunsinane and the tyrant falls to the man 'not of woman born'.
plot_or_argument: The prophecies kindle Macbeth's ambition and Lady Macbeth steels him to the murder; the crown brings only sleeplessness and escalating violence; Lady Macbeth's sleepwalking confession and death precede the final battle, where the equivocations of the witches are fulfilled and Macduff beheads the tyrant.
narrative_structure: A single-line tragedy of mounting speed, structured by the three prophecies and their ironic fulfilments, with the banquet scene as its turning point and the sleepwalking scene as its moral climax.
principal_characters: Macbeth; Lady Macbeth; Banquo; the Weird Sisters; Duncan; Macduff; Lady Macduff; Malcolm; Donalbain; Ross; Lennox; the Porter; Fleance
meter_and_prosody: The densest verse in Shakespeare — image packed and accelerated — with the witches' tetrameter charms and the Porter's prose as deliberate descents.
historical_context: Written 1606 for the new king, James I, the patron of the company and the author of Daemonologie; the play's Scottish matter, witchcraft, and Banquo's royal line all court the Stuart interest.
literary_significance: The supreme English tragedy of evil's self-entrapment — the shortest road to the heart of darkness the stage has ever built.
attribution_notes: Uncontested; the Hecate scenes may be later interpolations (possibly by Middleton).
bibliographical_notes: First printed in the First Folio, 1623. Standard edition: The Oxford Shakespeare: The Complete Works, 2nd edition (2005).

title: Antony and Cleopatra
description: Shakespeare's tragedy of empire and desire: the ageing Antony, caught between Rome and Egypt, duty and Cleopatra, loses the world at Actium and, hearing the false report of her death, falls on his sword; Cleopatra, refusing Octavius's triumph, dies by the asp, and the play ends with the lovers' deaths transfigured into myth.
plot_or_argument: Antony's dalliance in Alexandria draws him back to Rome and the marriage to Octavia; the breach with Caesar sends him back to Cleopatra; the sea-fight at Actium is lost when she flies and he follows; his rage, her feigned death, his botched suicide, and her staged one complete the tragedy — 'I am fire and air' — with Caesar left to bury them side by side.
narrative_structure: A tragedy of scenes, not acts — forty-two rapid movements between Rome and Alexandria — in which the lovers' deaths are deliberately drawn out across the final acts as ceremony and apotheosis.
principal_characters: Mark Antony; Cleopatra; Octavius Caesar; Enobarbus; Octavia; Charmian; Iras; Lepidus; Pompey; Alexas; Eros; Dolabella; the Clown
meter_and_prosody: A hyperbolic, sensuous verse of superlatives — Enobarbus's barge speech its summit — with the prose of Egypt's court as the foil to Roman plainness.
historical_context: Written about 1606–07 from North's Plutarch, whose phrasing Shakespeare follows at the barge and the death scenes; the play's imperial themes shadow the Jacobean debate over empire and union.
literary_significance: The greatest English poem of erotic grandeur — the tragedy in which the lovers outgrow tragedy itself.
bibliographical_notes: First printed in the First Folio, 1623. Standard edition: The Oxford Shakespeare: The Complete Works, 2nd edition (2005).

title: Coriolanus
description: Shakespeare's tragedy of the aristocratic warrior against the people: Caius Martius, conqueror of Corioli and now 'Coriolanus', refuses to court the plebeians for the consulship, is banished by the tribunes, and joins his Volscian enemy Aufidius to march on Rome — until his mother Volumnia's plea in the Volscian camp breaks him, and his capitulation costs him his life at Aufidius's hands.
plot_or_argument: The grain riots open the play; Coriolanus wins his name at Corioli; the tribunes Brutus and Sicinius manoeuvre him into rage and banishment; he defects to Aufidius and leads the Volscian army to Rome's gates; Volumnia, Virgilia, and the boy plead with him; he yields — 'O mother, mother!' — and Aufidius's faction cuts him down in Corioli.
narrative_structure: A political tragedy built on the confrontation of the one and the many, with the plebeians' crowd-scenes as chorus and Volumnia's embassy as the play's reversal.
principal_characters: Caius Martius Coriolanus; Volumnia; Virgilia; Menenius Agrippa; Tullus Aufidius; Cominius; Titus Lartius; Brutus; Sicinius Velutus; young Martius; Valeria
meter_and_prosody: A hard, sinewy verse of contempt and defiance, with the fable of the belly as the play's emblem of the body politic.
historical_context: Written about 1607–08 amid the Midland grain riots and the Commons' assertiveness under James I; its class politics have made it the most divisive of the Roman plays in performance.
literary_significance: The most rigorously political of the tragedies — a study of pride, populism, and the state that speaks with undiminished force to every later oligarchy.
bibliographical_notes: First printed in the First Folio, 1623. Standard edition: The Oxford Shakespeare: The Complete Works, 2nd edition (2005).

title: Timon of Athens
description: Shakespeare's (with Thomas Middleton's) unfinished-seeming tragedy of misanthropy: the prodigal Timon of Athens bankrupts himself in bounty, is abandoned by his flatterers, and retires to the woods to curse Athens and mankind — digging for roots and finding gold, which he flings to the whores, thieves, and the general Alcibiades, whose sack of Athens the play leaves hanging.
plot_or_argument: Timon's feasts and gifts draw the parasites; his creditors call; his friends refuse him; at his last banquet he serves them warm water and curses them; in the woods his gold draws a new parade of leeches; Alcibiades marches on Athens; and the play ends with Timon's epitaph and the city's submission, its loose ends never fully tied.
narrative_structure: A two-movement structure — Athens and the woods — with the masque of the false banquet as hinge; the play's rough edges suggest an abandoned draft revised for the press.
principal_characters: Timon; Flavius; Apemantus; Alcibiades; the Poet; the Painter; Lucullus; Lucius; Sempronius; Phrynia; Timandra; the Fool
meter_and_prosody: A verse of savage curses — Timon's tirades against gold and mankind are its glory — with the prose of the flatterers' scenes.
historical_context: Probably written about 1605–08, in the phase of Lear and Coriolanus; its satire of the Jacobean credit economy has made it a favourite of economic criticism.
literary_significance: The most extreme of the tragedies — a play of pure negation that has found its moment in every age of financial crisis.
attribution_notes: Thomas Middleton's share (the banquet scene and parts of the middle acts) is generally accepted on stylistic evidence.
bibliographical_notes: First printed in the First Folio, 1623. Standard edition: The Oxford Shakespeare: The Complete Works, 2nd edition (2005).

title: Pericles, Prince of Tyre
description: The first of the late romances, written with George Wilkins: the wanderings of Pericles, who flees Antiochus's riddle, wins Thaisa at Pentapolis, loses her in childbirth at sea, leaves their daughter Marina at Tarsus, and — after shipwreck, brothel, and the years of grief — is reunited with both in the recognition scenes at Mytilene and Diana's temple at Ephesus.
plot_or_argument: Pericles solves the incest riddle and flees; he wins Thaisa in the tournament; Thaisa 'dies' at sea and is revived at Ephesus; Marina is raised at Tarsus and saved from murder by pirates; the brothel scenes test her virtue; and the double recognition — father and daughter, then husband and wife — restores the family under Diana's guidance.
narrative_structure: An episodic sea-romance narrated and moralized by the poet Gower, who returns as chorus, in a deliberately archaic structure of storms, riddles, and reunions.
principal_characters: Pericles; Thaisa; Marina; Gower (the Chorus); Antiochus; Cleon; Dionyza; Simonides; Lysimachus; Cerimon; the Bawd; Boult; Diana
meter_and_prosody: Gower's tetrameter choruses frame a prose-and-verse play of variable texture, reflecting its joint authorship.
historical_context: Based on the Apollonius of Tyre story via Gower's Confessio Amantis and Lawrence Twine's prose version; the play was a popular success, printed in 1609 and omitted from the First Folio.
literary_significance: The gateway to the late romances — the play in which Shakespeare turned from tragedy to the art of restoration.
attribution_notes: Collaboration with George Wilkins for the first two acts is now generally accepted; the Folio omitted the play, which entered the canon in the Third Folio (1664).
bibliographical_notes: Quarto, 1609. Standard edition: The Oxford Shakespeare: The Complete Works, 2nd edition (2005).

title: Cymbeline
description: Shakespeare's romance of ancient Britain: Imogen, married secretly to the low-born Posthumus, is slandered by the villain Iachimo's wager; banished and betrayed, she flees in disguise as the boy Fidele to Wales, where her lost brothers live in the cave of Belarius; the Roman war, the dream of Jupiter, and the final scene's cascade of recognitions restore the family and the kingdom.
plot_or_argument: Iachimo hides in Imogen's trunk to 'prove' her infidelity; Posthumus orders her death; Pisanio spares her and she flees; the potion's mock-death, the cave, and Cloten's pursuit lead to the war with Rome; Posthumus fights for Britain in disguise; and the last scene unravels every knot — brothers, husband, father, and the tribute of peace.
narrative_structure: A romance of three worlds — court, Wales, Rome — braided into the single great recognition scene of Act 5, with the wager-plot from Boccaccio at its centre.
principal_characters: Imogen (Fidele); Posthumus Leonatus; Cymbeline; the Queen; Cloten; Iachimo; Pisanio; Belarius; Guiderius; Arviragus; Caius Lucius; Jupiter (in the apparition)
meter_and_prosody: A late style of extreme compression and ellipsis, with the dirge 'Fear no more the heat o' the sun' and the vision of Jupiter as its lyric heights.
historical_context: Written about 1609–10 from Holinshed's British matter and Boccaccio; its peace with Rome mirrors James I's pacific foreign policy.
literary_significance: The most experimental of the romances — a laboratory of plot whose final scene outdoes all its rivals in the theatre of recognition.
bibliographical_notes: First printed in the First Folio, 1623. Standard edition: The Oxford Shakespeare: The Complete Works, 2nd edition (2005).

title: The Winter's Tale
description: Shakespeare's romance of jealousy and resurrection: Leontes of Sicilia, seized by groundless suspicion, destroys his queen Hermione and orders the exposure of their newborn daughter; the child Perdita grows up a shepherd's daughter in Bohemia; sixteen years later the flight to Sicilia, the revelation of her birth, and the 'statue' scene bring Hermione back to life and the family together again.
plot_or_argument: Leontes' sudden jealousy condemns Hermione; the oracle's verdict comes too late and the prince dies of grief; Perdita is exposed and found; the Bohemian pastoral of the sheep-shearing and the courtship of Florizel occupy the middle acts; the flight to Sicilia unravels Perdita's birth; and Paulina reveals Hermione, preserved in secret, in the play's miraculous final scene.
narrative_structure: A two-part structure — tragedy in Sicilia, pastoral in Bohemia — bridged by Time the Chorus and resolved in the resurrection ending, with the bear's exit as the most famous stage direction in English.
principal_characters: Leontes; Hermione; Perdita; Florizel; Polixenes; Paulina; Camillo; Antigonus; Autolycus; the Old Shepherd; the Clown; Time (the Chorus); Mamillius
meter_and_prosody: The late style at its richest — the flower speeches of Perdita, the ballads of Autolycus — with the trial scene's forensic verse as the tragic core.
historical_context: Written about 1610–11 from Greene's Pandosto; performed at court in 1611 and at the Globe; the statue scene's art-life paradox crowns Shakespeare's last engagement with Ovid and Pygmalion.
literary_significance: The most moving of the romances — the play of grace, time, and forgiveness that defined the tragicomic art of the late Shakespeare.
bibliographical_notes: First printed in the First Folio, 1623. Standard edition: The Oxford Shakespeare: The Complete Works, 2nd edition (2005).

title: The Tempest
description: Shakespeare's farewell to the stage: Prospero, the deposed Duke of Milan, has raised the storm that wrecks his enemies on his island; with his spirit Ariel and the enslaved Caliban, he conducts the shipwrecked court through the play's ordeals to repentance, wins the betrothal of his daughter Miranda to Ferdinand, breaks his staff, and sails for Milan — 'our revels now are ended'.
plot_or_argument: The tempest delivers Alonso's court to Prospero's island; Ferdinand and Miranda meet and are tested; Caliban, Stephano, and Trinculo plot their drunken coup; Ariel's banquet harrows the 'three men of sin'; and the final scene forgives all — with Caliban left to 'seek for grace' and Prospero to drown his book.
narrative_structure: The most classical of the plays — a single island, a single day, a masque at its centre — shaped as Prospero's design from storm to pardon.
principal_characters: Prospero; Miranda; Ariel; Caliban; Ferdinand; Alonso; Antonio; Sebastian; Gonzalo; Stephano; Trinculo; Sycorax (reported); Juno, Ceres, and Iris (in the masque)
meter_and_prosody: The late verse at its most musical — Ariel's songs, the masque, the 'cloud-capped towers' speech — with Caliban's prose and the sailors' comedy as counterpoint.
historical_context: Performed at court, 1 November 1611, and for the wedding of Princess Elizabeth in 1613; its New World echoes draw on the Virginia pamphlets and the wreck of the Sea Venture (1609).
literary_significance: Shakespeare's valediction — the play that has served every later age as a fable of art, empire, and forgiveness, and the most reinterpreted text in the canon.
bibliographical_notes: First printed in the First Folio, 1623. Standard edition: The Oxford Shakespeare: The Complete Works, 2nd edition (2005).

title: The Two Noble Kinsmen
description: Shakespeare's last play, written with John Fletcher from Chaucer's Knight's Tale: the cousins Palamon and Arcite, kinsmen and friends, both fall in love with Emilia from their prison window; their rivalry is settled by the tournament for her hand — Arcite wins and dies in a riding accident, and Palamon marries her, while the Jailer's Daughter's mad sub-plot runs its course.
plot_or_argument: The cousins swear eternal friendship, then break it over Emilia; Arcite is released, Palamon escapes; the tournament appoints the winner; Arcite's victory is followed by his fatal fall from the horse; the dying Arcite bequeaths Emilia to Palamon; Theseus closes the play on the riddle of fortune, while the Jailer's Daughter is cured by the doctor's masque of her wooer.
narrative_structure: A tragicomedy of friendship and fortune in five acts, with the Jailer's Daughter's madness as a tragic sub-plot and the Morris dance and tournament as spectacle.
principal_characters: Palamon; Arcite; Emilia; Theseus; Hippolyta; the Jailer; the Jailer's Daughter; the Wooer; Pirithous; the Doctor
meter_and_prosody: The collaboration's two styles are audibly joined — Shakespeare's ceremonial verse (the prayers at the altars) with Fletcher's supple fluency.
historical_context: First performed about 1614, after the Globe fire, probably at Blackfriars; printed in quarto in 1634 as 'by the memorable worthies... Mr John Fletcher and Mr William Shakespeare'; omitted from the First Folio.
literary_significance: The closing chord of the Shakespeare canon — a return to Chaucer, and to the question of friendship and love with which his career began.
attribution_notes: Joint authorship with John Fletcher is established on title-page and stylistic evidence and is universally accepted; the division of scenes is broadly agreed.
bibliographical_notes: Quarto, 1634. Standard edition: The Oxford Shakespeare: The Complete Works, 2nd edition (2005).
